The '''60th Academy Awards''' ceremony, presented by the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS), took place on April 11, 1988, at the [[Shrine Auditorium]] in Los Angeles beginning at 6:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PDT]]. During the ceremony, AMPAS presented [[Academy Awards]] (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 22 categories honoring [[1987 in film|films released in 1987]]. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], was produced by [[Samuel Goldwyn Jr.]] and directed by Marty Pasetta.<ref name=VanGelder /><ref>{{cite news|last1=Caulfield |first1=Deborah |title=TV & Video |url=https://articles.latimes.com/keyword/marty-pasetta |access-date=July 1, 2014 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=December 7, 1987 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715023021/http://articles.latimes.com/keyword/marty-pasetta |archive-date=July 15, 2014 }}</ref> Actor [[Chevy Chase]] hosted the show for the second consecutive year.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Gilatto|first1=Tom|title=Oscar Wild|work=[[USA Today]]|date=January 27, 1988}}</ref> Two weeks earlier, in a ceremony held at [[the Beverly Hilton]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], on March 27, the [[Academy Award for Technical Achievement|Academy Awards for Technical Achievement]] were presented by host [[Shirley Jones]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Past Scientific & Technical Awards Ceremonies|url=http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|access-date=July 31, 2013|publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140213185729/http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|archive-date=February 13, 2014}}</ref>

''[[The Last Emperor]]'' won all nine awards it was nominated for, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]] and [[Academy Award for Best Director|Best Director]] for [[Bernardo Bertolucci]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Harmetz|first=Aljean|author-link=Aljean Harmetz|title=''The Last Emperor'' Wins 9 Oscars and Is Named Best Film of 1987|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/04/12/movies/the-last-emperor-wins-9-oscars-and-is-named-best-film-of-1987.html|access-date=July 3, 2014|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 12, 1988|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714220510/http://www.nytimes.com/1988/04/12/movies/the-last-emperor-wins-9-oscars-and-is-named-best-film-of-1987.html|archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref> For their performances in ''[[Moonstruck]]'', [[Cher]] and [[Olympia Dukakis]] won [[Academy Award for Best Actress|Best Actress]] and [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress|Best Supporting Actress]], respectively. [[Michael Douglas]] won [[Academy Award for Best Actor|Best Actor]] for his role in ''[[Wall Street (1987 film)|Wall Street]]''; and [[Sean Connery]] won [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor|Best Supporting Actor]] for ''[[The Untouchables (film)|The Untouchables]]'', the latter becoming the [[List of Academy Award winners and nominees from Great Britain#Best Actor in a Supporting Role|first and only Scottish thespian to win an acting Oscar]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Cieply |first=Michael |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-12-mn-783-story.html |title=''Last Emperor'' Reigns Over Oscar Ceremonies : Best Picture Winner Adds Eight Other Awards; Cher and Douglas Take Top Prizes for Acting |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 12, 1988 |access-date=June 4, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130627083448/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-04-12/news/mn-783_1_picture-winner |archive-date=June 27, 2013 }}</ref> The telecast garnered 42.2&nbsp;million viewers in the United States.

==Winners and nominees==
The nominees for the 60th Academy Awards were announced on February 16, 1988, at 5:38&nbsp;PM [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]] (13:38 [[Universal Time Coordinated|UTC]]) at the [[Samuel Goldwyn Theater]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], by [[Robert Wise]], president of the academy, and actress [[Shirley MacLaine]].{{sfn|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=712}} ''[[The Last Emperor]]'' received the most nominations, with nine total; ''[[Broadcast News (film)|Broadcast News]]'' came in second with seven.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Cieply |first1=Michael |title='Emperor' Leads Topsy-Turvy Oscar Race : American Directors Are Shut Out for the First Time in Academy History |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-02-18-ca-43482-story.html |access-date=February 24, 2008 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=February 16, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715015448/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-02-18/entertainment/ca-43482_1_emperor-leads-topsy-turvy-oscar-race |archive-date=July 15, 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Ryan |first1=Desmond |title=The Oscar Nominees ''The Last Emperor'' and ''Broadcast News'' Lead the Field|url=http://articles.philly.com/1988-02-18/news/26240453_1_nominations-oscars-fatal-attraction |access-date=July 8, 2014 |work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] |date=February 18, 1988 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714203101/http://articles.philly.com/1988-02-18/news/26240453_1_nominations-oscars-fatal-attraction |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref>

The winners were announced at the awards ceremony on April 11, 1988.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gorney |first1=Cynthia |title=Douglas and Cher Win Acting Honors |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1988/04/12/douglas-and-cher-win-acting-honors/a61f1eb8-6ca5-4b8e-b25d-8d0bb24c2242/ |access-date=June 29, 2020 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=April 12, 1988 |archive-date=June 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200629175814/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1988/04/12/douglas-and-cher-win-acting-honors/a61f1eb8-6ca5-4b8e-b25d-8d0bb24c2242/ |url-status=live }}</ref> ''The Last Emperor'' became the second film after 1958's ''[[Gigi (1958 film)|Gigi]]'' to earn nine Oscar nominations and win all of them.<ref>{{cite news|title=Some achievement, but not a record|work=[[Vancouver Sun]]|date=April 16, 1988|page=D1}}</ref> For the first time in Oscar history, all five Best Director nominees were born outside the United States.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Cieply |first1=Michael |title=No Oscars for U.S. Directors : Foreigners Win All Nominations; 9 for ''Last Emperor''|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-02-17-mn-29431-story.html |access-date=July 1, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=February 17, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714201447/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-02-17/news/mn-29431_1_broadcast-news |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> Best Actor winner Michael Douglas became the first person to win Oscars for both acting and producing, albeit the first person to win the awards for two separate films and in different years. He previously won a Best Picture award as co-producer of ''[[One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (film)|One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest]]'' (1975).<ref name="BEDO">{{cite news|last1=Crook |first1=John |title=Like Father, Like Son at the Golden Globes |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-jan-25-tv-coverstory25-story.html |access-date=November 23, 2015 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=January 25, 2004 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151123142037/http://articles.latimes.com/2004/jan/25/news/tv-coverstory25 |archive-date=November 23, 2015 }}</ref>

===Special Achievement Award (Sound Effects Editing)===
* ''[[RoboCop]]'' – [[Stephen Hunter Flick|Stephen Flick]] and [[John Pospisil]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Special Oscar Goes To 'RoboCop' Effects|work=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] |date=February 18, 1988|page=E1}}</ref>

===Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award===
The award honors "creative producers whose bodies of work reflect a consistently high quality of motion picture production".<ref>{{cite news|title=Irvin G. Thalberg Memorial Award |url=http://www.oscars.org/governors/thalberg |access-date=December 18, 2015 |publisher=Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160101224449/http://oscars.org/governors/thalberg |archive-date=January 1, 2016 }}</ref>
*[[Billy Wilder]]<ref name="Thalberg">{{cite news|title=Billy Wilder to Receive The Thalberg Award |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/02/14/movies/billy-wilder-to-receive-the-thalberg-award.html |access-date=July 1, 2014 |work=The New York Times |date=February 14, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714205053/http://www.nytimes.com/1988/02/14/movies/billy-wilder-to-receive-the-thalberg-award.html |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref>

==Ceremony information==
[[File:Chevy Chase (1990).jpg|thumb|130px|right|[[Chevy Chase]] hosted the 60th Academy Awards.|alt=Photo of Chevy Chase attending the 62 Academy Awards in 1990.]]

In view of the 60th anniversary of the Academy Awards, the academy hired film producer [[Samuel Goldwyn Jr.]] in October 1987 to oversee the telecast for the second straight year.<ref name=VanGelder>{{cite news|first=Lawrence|last=Van Gelder|author-link=Lawrence Van Gelder|title=At the Movies|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/10/30/movies/at-the-movies.html|access-date=December 18, 2015|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=October 30, 1987|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222211728/http://www.nytimes.com/1987/10/30/movies/at-the-movies.html |archive-date=December 22, 2015}}</ref> Three months later, Goldwyn selected actor and comedian [[Chevy Chase]] to emcee the 1988 ceremony.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Schnurmacher|first1=Thomas|title=SPAC, SPCA ask VIPs to RSVP ASAP|work=[[Montreal Gazette]] |date=January 18, 1988|page=C9}}</ref> In addition, after being held at the [[Dorothy Chandler Pavilion]] for almost two decades, AMPAS decided to move the telecast to the [[Shrine Auditorium]] in order to accommodate more rehearsal time and take advantage of the large venue's seating capacity.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Culhane |first1=John |title=With Help From Friends, Oscar's a Wit and Raconteur |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/04/10/movies/with-help-from-friends-oscar-s-a-wit-and-raconteur.html |access-date=July 3, 2014 |work=The New York Times |date=April 10, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140203222104/http://www.nytimes.com/1988/04/10/movies/with-help-from-friends-oscar-s-a-wit-and-raconteur.html |archive-date=February 3, 2014 }}</ref> This marked the first time the facility served as the site for the Oscars since the [[20th Academy Awards|20th ceremony]] held in 1948.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Voland |first1=John |title=Oscar's Life Complicated by Writers' Strike, New Setting |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-08-ca-1014-story.html |access-date=July 2, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 8, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714195457/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-04-08/entertainment/ca-1014_1_guild-strike-rules/2 |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> Additionally, Goldwyn and Passetta originally planned to feature pre-recorded red carpet arrival footage of actors who had roles in the 59 previous Best Picture winners. However, the segment was dropped altogether due to traffic problems among guests arriving at the ceremony.{{sfn|Osborne|2008|p=287}}<ref>{{cite news|last1=Caulfield |first1=Deborah |title=First Off... |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-13-ca-745-story.html |access-date=3 July 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 11, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714232959/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-04-13/entertainment/ca-745_1_traffic-jam |archive-date=14 July 2014 }}</ref>

Furthermore, the [[1988 Writers Guild of America strike]], which began more than a month before the ceremony, affected the telecast and its surrounding events. Despite the [[Writers Guild of America, West|Writers Guild of America]] refusing to grant a waiver permitting writers to work on the scripted dialogue for the gala, the three head writers for the telecast, [[Ernest Lehman]], [[Melville Shavelson]], and [[Jack Rose (screenwriter)|Jack Rose]], assured the AMPAS and ABC that more than half of the material had already been completed.<ref name="Strike Experience">{{cite news|last1=Killday |title=Oscar has experience with strike-related uncertainty |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/oscar-has-experience-strike-related-104329 |access-date=February 3, 2014 |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=February 8, 2008 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714123409/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/oscar-has-experience-strike-related-104329 |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> To compensate for the missing portions of the script, Goldwyn heavily utilized comedians such as [[John Candy]], [[Billy Crystal]], [[Eddie Murphy]], and [[Robin Williams]] to [[ad lib]] and improvise jokes.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Spillman|first1=Susan|title=Hope and glory at the Oscars|work=USA Today |date=April 11, 1988|page=4D}}</ref>{{sfn|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=716}} During the show, many of the participants expressed support for the writers, such as Best Supporting Actor winner [[Sean Connery]] who remarked in his acceptance speech, "If such a thing as a wish accompanied this award mine would be that we ended the writers' strike."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Voland |first1=John |title=This Year, Most of the Thanks Go to Writers |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-12-ca-969-story.html |access-date=July 2, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 12, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714125141/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-04-12/entertainment/ca-969_1_writers |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref>

===Box office performance of nominated films===
At the time of the nominations announcement on February 16, the combined gross of the five Best Picture nominees at the US box office was $221&nbsp;million with an average of $48.9&nbsp;million.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars>{{cite news|title=1989 Academy Award Nominations and Winner for Best Picture |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1987&p=.htm |access-date=June 17, 2014 |website=[[Box Office Mojo]] ([[Amazon.com]]) |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140614052150/http://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1987&p=.htm |archive-date=June 14, 2014 }}</ref> ''Fatal Attraction'' was the highest earner among the Best Picture nominees, with $142&nbsp;million in domestic box office receipts. The film was followed by ''Broadcast News'' ($36.7&nbsp;million), ''Moonstruck'' ($25.4&nbsp;million), ''The Last Emperor'' ($11.9&nbsp;million), and ''Hope and Glory'' ($5.2&nbsp;million).<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/>

Of the 50 highest-grossing movies of the year, 39 nominations went to 17 films on the list. Only ''Fatal Attraction'' (2nd), ''The Untouchables'' (4th), ''Good Morning Vietnam'' (10th), ''Throw Momma from the Train'' (14th), ''Full Metal Jacket'' (21st), ''Broadcast News'' (26th), ''Wall Street'' (30th), and ''Moonstruck'' (39th) were nominated for Best Picture, acting, directing, or screenwriting. The other top 50 box office hits that earned nominations were ''Beverly Hills Cop II'' (1st), ''Lethal Weapon'' (7th), ''The Witches of Eastwick'' (8th), ''Dirty Dancing'' (9th), ''Predator'' (11th), ''RoboCop'' (15th), ''Mannequin'' (23rd), ''The Princess Bride'' (38th), and ''Innerspace'' (45th).<ref>{{cite news|title=1987 Box Office Grosses (as of February 15, 1988) |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1988-02-15&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1987&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |access-date=July 1, 2014 |website=Box Office Mojo (Amazon.com) |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140719002751/http://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1988-02-15&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1987&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |archive-date=July 19, 2014 }}</ref>

===Critical reviews===
The telecast received a negative reception from media outlets. ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' television critic [[Howard Rosenberg]] commented, "Monday night's Academy Awards telecast on ABC was the [[Michael Dukakis]] and [[George H. W. Bush|George Bush]] of TV awards programs: parched, drab and leaden. You kept hoping they'd draft [[Mario Cuomo]]."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Rosenberg |first1=Howard |title=A Night With All the Excitement of an Envelope Opening |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-12-ca-964-story.html |access-date=July 2, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 12, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714164017/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-04-12/entertainment/ca-964_1_envelope-opening |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> Tom Shales from ''[[The Washington Post]]'' wrote, "Of hope there was little and of glory almost none last night at the 60th annual Academy Awards, telecast live from the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles on ABC. Even considering the low standards set in previous years, the program seemed unusually lackluster from the word go."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Shales|first1=Tom|title=A Tortured New Look In Hollywood Horror|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=April 12, 1988}}</ref> Columnist Matt Roush of ''[[USA Today]]'' quipped, "Chevy Chase stopped the show. Cold. Over and over. As the ever-unctuous host, he tried to get laughs by picking his nose and sneezing into his hand when his ad-libs failed, which was often." He also observed that ''[[The Last Emperor]]'' dominance over the awards created a dull and anticlimactic atmosphere to the proceedings.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Roush|first1=Matt|title=A show short on surprises|work=USA Today |date=April 12, 1988}}</ref>

===Ratings and reception===
The American telecast on ABC drew in an average of 42.2&nbsp;million people over its length, which was a 13% increase from the [[59th Academy Awards|previous year's ceremony]].<ref name="LATrating">{{cite news|last=Voland |first=John |title=TV RATINGS : Oscars Lead the Ratings Race  |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-20-ca-1198-story.html |access-date=April 25, 2026 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 20, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260425173051/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-20-ca-1198-story.html |archive-date=April 25, 2026 }}</ref> An estimated 70&nbsp;million total viewers watched all or part of the awards.<ref>{{cite news|title=Oscars Push ABC to Win Ratings Race |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-04-03-ca-864-story.html |access-date=June 6, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 3, 1990 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140711022630/http://articles.latimes.com/1990-04-03/entertainment/ca-864_1_ratings-race |archive-date=July 11, 2014 }}</ref> The show also drew higher [[Nielsen ratings]] compared to the previous ceremony, with 29.2% of households over a 49 percent share.<ref name="LATrating"/><ref>{{cite news|title=ABC gets an Oscar boost|work=USA Today|page=3D |date=April 4, 1990}}</ref>

In July 1988, the ceremony presentation received four nominations at the [[40th Primetime Emmy Awards|40th Primetime Emmy]]s.<ref>{{cite news|title=Nominations for Prime-Time Emmys |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-07-29-ca-8047-story.html |access-date=July 1, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=July 28, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714222151/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-07-29/entertainment/ca-8047_1_great-performances |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Primetime Emmy Award database |url=http://www.emmys.com/shows/60th-annual-academy-awards |access-date=April 29, 2014 |publisher=[[Academy of Television Arts & Sciences]] (ATAS) |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714205610/http://www.emmys.com/shows/60th-annual-academy-awards |archive-date=July 14, 2014 }}</ref> The following month, the ceremony won one of those nominations for Outstanding Variety Music Events Programming (Samuel Goldwyn, Jr.).<ref>{{cite news|last1=Margulies |first1=Lee |title=Cable Gets Prime-Time Emmys |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-08-25-ca-1277-story.html |access-date=May 19, 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715043636/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-08-25/entertainment/ca-1277_1_cable-program |archive-date=July 15, 2014 }}</ref>
